summary.text: 水 pictures flowing water: a central current flanked by marks for droplets. Its basic and common meaning is “water.”

formation.text: The whole graph is pictographic: its central line represents a current, and the side marks represent droplets. A Han-era explanation adds a cosmological account, which is a historical interpretation rather than a breakdown of the graph into components.

history.text: Oracle-script forms vary in their side marks. Bronze and Warring States forms retain the flowing-water picture. The selected oracle-script and Western Zhou bronze-script glyphs are modern vector redrawings, not photographs of artifacts.
A Han-era account glosses 水 as “level” and explains it through the cosmology of the time. This is a historical explanation of the graph and word, distinct from its pictorial construction.

uncertainties.text: The supplied proposals for the spoken word’s earlier pronunciation and its possible connections to other languages differ and remain unresolved; they do not identify a phonetic component in 水.

senses.period: Shang oracle-bone examples; individual dates unresolved
senses.text: Reported Shang oracle-bone examples use 水 for water or flooding. This is the earliest meaning supported here.
The common current meaning is “water.” Other glosses include liquid, lotion, and juice; their chronology is not established here.
A bronze inscription is reported to use 水 to write the different word 乞, “request.” This is graph borrowing, not a development of the meaning “water” into “request.”
One reported oracle-bone use has been read as a verb involving either leveling ground with water or washing a temple. Its reading and relation to the noun “water” remain unresolved.

developments.text: The graph was reportedly reused to write 乞, “request,” on the proposed basis that the words sounded alike or similarly. The match is unverified; the old name of the pictured water and a historical sound comparison for both words are not established here.

limitations.text: The oracle-bone examples and their individual dates are not specified in detail here. The relation between the disputed verbal use and the noun “water” is unresolved.
The proposed sound-based explanation for using 水 to write 乞 is not confirmed by a historical comparison of the two words’ pronunciations.

水準 is reported in a compound meaning “leveling instrument” and in an abstract sense meaning “standard” or “level.” Those compound meanings do not establish separate senses of 水, and their stages are undated here.

overview.text: 水 pictures flowing water, with a central current and marks for droplets. Its common meaning is “water.”
